Text:
Three of the eight presumptive signs of death are the ones the primary assessment itself turns up:

{{c1::unresponsiveness to painful stimuli}}

{{c1::lack of a carotid pulse or heartbeat}}

{{c1::absence of chest rise and fall}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: presumptive signs carry the most weight when they follow a severe trauma or occur at the end stage of a long illness such as cancer; nothing about them is conclusive on its own.

Roster: Unresponsiveness to painful stimuli · Lack of a carotid pulse or heartbeat · Absence of chest rise and fall · No deep tendon or corneal reflexes · Absence of pupillary reactivity · No systolic blood pressure · Profound cyanosis · Lowered or decreased body temperature

Text:
Three of the eight presumptive signs of death appear only when you deliberately test for them:

{{c1::no deep tendon or corneal reflexes}}

{{c1::absence of pupillary reactivity}}

{{c1::no systolic blood pressure}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: a presumptive sign is presumed, not proven — in sudden death from hypothermia, acute poisoning, or cardiac arrest, more evidence is needed before death is assumed.

Roster: Unresponsiveness to painful stimuli · Lack of a carotid pulse or heartbeat · Absence of chest rise and fall · No deep tendon or corneal reflexes · Absence of pupillary reactivity · No systolic blood pressure · Profound cyanosis · Lowered or decreased body temperature

Text:
Two of the eight presumptive signs of death are read off the body itself rather than from any test:

{{c1::profound cyanosis}}

{{c1::lowered or decreased body temperature}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: a lowered body temperature only suggests death, whereas algor mortis — the body cooled all the way to the surrounding temperature — is a definitive sign, alongside obvious mortal damage, dependent lividity, and rigor mortis.

Roster: Unresponsiveness to painful stimuli · Lack of a carotid pulse or heartbeat · Absence of chest rise and fall · No deep tendon or corneal reflexes · Absence of pupillary reactivity · No systolic blood pressure · Profound cyanosis · Lowered or decreased body temperature

Text:
Two of the eight decision-making capacity factors are about the patient's standing before the call ever began:

{{c1::intellectual capacity impaired by mental limitation or dementia}}

{{c1::being of legal age, 18 years old in most states}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: decision-making capacity is the health care term for whether a patient can understand and process what you are telling him, whereas competence is a legal term and a court decides it.

Roster: Impaired intellect (mental limitation or dementia) · Legal age · Alcohol or drug intoxication, or serious injury or illness · Significant pain · A significant distracting injury · Hearing or visual problems · A language barrier · Apparent understanding

Text:
Three of the eight decision-making capacity factors ask what is clouding the patient at this moment:

{{c1::alcohol or drug intoxication, or serious injury or illness}}

{{c1::significant pain}}

{{c1::a significant injury that distracts from a more serious one}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: a significant non-life-threatening injury can cause extreme pain and distract the patient from neck pain that signals a far more serious problem.

Roster: Impaired intellect (mental limitation or dementia) · Legal age · Alcohol or drug intoxication, or serious injury or illness · Significant pain · A significant distracting injury · Hearing or visual problems · A language barrier · Apparent understanding

Text:
Three of the eight decision-making capacity factors ask whether you and the patient can communicate at all:

{{c1::apparent hearing or visual problems}}

{{c1::a language barrier}}

{{c1::apparent understanding, shown by rational questions}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: a hearing, vision, or language problem stops the information from reaching the patient, whereas a lack of apparent understanding means it arrived and was not processed.

Roster: Impaired intellect (mental limitation or dementia) · Legal age · Alcohol or drug intoxication, or serious injury or illness · Significant pain · A significant distracting injury · Hearing or visual problems · A language barrier · Apparent understanding
